newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italian strike - Fiat says support slipping.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italian strike - Fiat says support slipping.

text.p: Italian engineering and metal workers staged a mass demonstration in Rome on Friday to press their demands in bitter pay dispute but carmaker Fiat said support for the protest on the shop floor was slipping.

Trades unions said more than 150,000 workers, staging their second one-day strike in two months, converged in central Rome to protest at management's refusal to compensate in full for higher-than-expected inflation in the past contractual period.

In cash terms, unions want a gross 262,000 lire ($175) rise in their monthly pay packets, of which 97,000 is to cover the overrun in inflation between 1994 and 1996. Employers have offered 195,000 lire of which just 30,000 is for inflation.

"They gave (Formula One driver Michael) Schumacher 42 billion lire ($28 million) but they won't give us 262,000 lire," said Roberto Manzi, deputy mayor of Gessopolone, a town in the central Abruzzo region where Fiat have a truck factory.
He was referring to a deal recently signed by former world champion Schumacher with Ferrari, which is owned by the Agnelli family who also control Fiat.

Some 1,700 coaches and 25 special trains brought workers from around Italy to the protest but Fiat said the strikers, who blew whistles and waved banners in the square of St John's Lateran, were losing support on the shop floor.
Fiat said 10 percent less of its total work force joined in the protest compared with a similar strike on September 27.
It said its Mirafiori car plant in Turin saw 19 percent of the work force striking in its car body shop, 29 percent on its assembly lines, and 18 percent in its press works.
Figures from three southern plants showed about 25 percent of workers took part in the demonstration but in other areas the strike levels were higher than in September.

The metalwork sector forms the core of Italian industry and accounts for about 40 percent of total manufacturing output. Besides Fiat, technology group Olivetti and state shipbuilders Fincantieri were also affected by the strike.

Contracts for the sector's 1.7 million workers expired at the end of June but employers and unions have failed to agree on new terms. The two sides last held talks back in September and no new meeting is planned.
Non-ferrous mines, smelters and refineries were not affected by Friday's stoppages.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government has said that if the employers' association, Federmeccanica, does not return to the bargaining table by November 28 it will intervene in the dispute and try to find a settlement.
To support the metalworkers, unions have called a strike for December 13 in the industrial and transport sectors.

At the heart of the protracted dispute lies a battle over how to interpret a landmark 1993 labour accord which scrapped automatic index-linking of salaries provided management made up any shortfall in wages if inflation ran above target.
But the wording of the deal was vague. Unions interpret it to mean that all the inflation overshoot should be covered. Management argue only a part of lost earnings need be made up.
The employers have found an ally in the Bank of Italy which said last month that unions were not considering recent falls in inflation and should temper their demands.
Provisional data on Thursday showed annual inflation in November at 2.6 percent against six percent 12 months ago.
"If we met the workers' demands, inflation would hit four or five percent," Innocenzo Cipolletta, director general of industrialists' association Confindustria, told reporters.
